annotation_description: Playing Mountain instead of Thundering Falls on turn 1 is suboptimal. Thundering Falls enters tapped, so playing it on turn 1 (when you want to cast Ragavan on turn 1 anyway but can't off Thundering Falls) means you lose nothing by playing it now and having it untapped on turn 2. However, the key issue is that playing Mountain turn 1 enables casting Ragavan turn 1 (which is the best play in Modern), so Mountain is actually correct IF you plan to cast Ragavan this turn. But wait - looking at the hand, the player HAS Ragavan and Mountain produces R, so playing Mountain and casting Ragavan turn 1 is the right line. The question is whether the player will follow through with casting Ragavan. If they do, Mountain is correct. If they play Thundering Falls instead, they'd lose the tempo of a turn 1 Ragavan. Actually, Mountain is the correct play here to enable turn 1 Ragavan, so this is not a blunder.

Playing Ifnir Deadlands instead of Prismatic Vista on turn 1 means paying 1 life every time black mana is needed from this land on future turns. With Emperor of Bones ({1}{B}) and multiple Thoughtseizes in hand, the player will need repeated black mana. Prismatic Vista would fetch a basic Swamp that taps for {B} for free every turn, saving multiple life points over the course of the game while also thinning the deck.

With Emperor of Bones in hand as a turn 2 play, and two Thoughtseizes available, taking one Ragavan still leaves the opponent with another Ragavan to deploy on turn 1. Taking Ephemerate might be stronger since it's the card that generates the most value with Phelia (repeated blink effects), and the second Thoughtseize could handle a Ragavan next turn. Alternatively, taking Phelia removes the most powerful mid-game threat that Ephemerate combos with. However, taking Ragavan is defensible since the opponent can still play the second Ragavan immediately next turn and generate tempo/card advantage before we can Thoughtseize again.

Played Thundering Falls (enters tapped) instead of Mountain, missing the opportunity to deploy Turn 1 Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer. Ragavan on Turn 1 is one of the strongest possible openings in Modern, generating card and mana advantage starting Turn 2. Playing the tapped land wastes the entire first turn.

Playing Prismatic Vista and cracking it costs 1 life unnecessarily when Eldrazi Temple (or Wastes) could produce the same mana needed this turn (Thoughtseize + Pithing Needle) without the life cost. Eldrazi Temple provides {C} for Pithing Needle while Ifnir Deadlands provides {B} for Thoughtseize, achieving the same double-spell turn.

Cast Pithing Needle before Thoughtseize when both could be cast this turn (Thoughtseize costs {B}, Needle costs {1}, and the player has {B}+{C} available). Casting Thoughtseize first would reveal the opponent's hand, allowing Pithing Needle to name the optimal card with perfect information. Instead, Pithing Needle must be named blind.

Opponent is on only 1 land, making 3-mana Teferi several turns away from being castable. Phelia (2 mana, flash) is the more immediate threat that could come down much sooner, exile Pithing Needle or Emperor of Bones when attacking, and combo with Ephemerate for repeated value.

Playing Mountain instead of Scalding Tarn. Unless Pithing Needle is naming Scalding Tarn (which is possible since opponent saw the hand via Thoughtseize), Scalding Tarn is generally the better land to play first - it provides flexibility to fetch whatever color is needed, thins the deck, and preserves Mountain in hand as a guaranteed untapped land for future turns.

annotation_description: Casting Ragavan without Dash means it doesn't have haste, so it can't attack this turn. The opponent has Pithing Needle on the battlefield (likely naming something relevant) and only 13 life. Dashing Ragavan for {1}{R} would give it haste, allowing it to attack this turn and potentially deal 2 damage plus generate a Treasure token and exile a card. However, the player only has 2 lands (Thundering Falls and Mountain), plus Scalding Tarn in hand. If they play Scalding Tarn and use it, they'd have 3 mana available - enough for Dash ({1}{R}) but then couldn't also cast Phelia ({1}{W}). The hardcast for {R} preserves mana to potentially play Scalding Tarn and cast Phelia ({1}{W}) this turn, getting two creatures on board. This is a reasonable consideration, but Ragavan without haste is vulnerable to removal and doesn't generate immediate value. The opponent is tapped out with only 2 lands, so the risk of removal is low this turn, but Ragavan is still a lightning rod. Playing Phelia alongside Ragavan gives two threats but neither attacks this turn. The decision is debatable but not clearly wrong.

Cast Thoughtseize before playing a land drop. Should always play land before casting spells to preserve maximum flexibility. Additionally, at 13 life with Ragavan threatening combat damage value, deploying Emperor of Bones (which blocks Ragavan and can start generating value from the stocked graveyards) may have been more impactful than a third Thoughtseize against a likely depleted hand.

Took Phelia when the opponent has no white mana to cast it, leaving Consign to Memory which is immediately castable with Thundering Falls and directly counters Emperor of Bones' critical triggered abilities (the combat exile trigger and the +1/+1 counter reanimation trigger). Consign to Memory is the most immediately threatening card against our game plan.

Playing Wastes instead of Eldrazi Temple is suboptimal. Eldrazi Temple produces {C} just like Wastes for general use, but also produces {C}{C} for colorless Eldrazi spells. With Emperor of Bones in hand (which costs {1}{B}), the Emperor isn't colorless so the Eldrazi Temple bonus doesn't apply to it directly. However, Eldrazi Temple is strictly better than Wastes in almost every scenario - it produces the same {C} normally, but has upside for any future Eldrazi spells or abilities. There's no reason to play Wastes over Eldrazi Temple when both are available, as Eldrazi Temple is a strict upgrade for the land drop.

Emperor of Bones should generally be cast after activating Mishra's Bauble first. The Bauble costs 0 mana to activate (tap + sacrifice) and provides information about the opponent's top card plus a delayed draw. There's no reason not to activate it before casting Emperor of Bones, since it's free and the draw will come at the next upkeep regardless. Additionally, activating Bauble before combat could provide useful information. By casting Emperor of Bones first, the player loses the option to activate Bauble during their own main phase (they can still do it later, but sequencing the free action first is strictly better as it preserves more options).

Ragavan has Pithing Needle naming it on the opponent's battlefield, which prevents its activated abilities (Dash) from being used. More importantly, Pithing Needle shuts down Ragavan's triggered ability from dealing combat damage - wait, actually Pithing Needle only stops activated abilities, not triggered abilities. However, casting Ragavan before combat when holding Ephemerate is questionable sequencing. But the bigger issue is that the player chose to cast Ragavan instead of activating Scalding Tarn first. By casting Ragavan (1 mana) using Mountain or Thundering Falls, they use their mana. But Scalding Tarn should be cracked to fetch a land to have more mana available or to thin the deck. Actually, looking more carefully: the choices are only 'Scalding Tarn' and 'Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer' - so the player can either crack the fetch or cast Ragavan. Casting Ragavan before cracking Scalding Tarn means if they want to attack with Ragavan and use Ephemerate (which costs W), they need a Plains. They should crack Scalding Tarn first to fetch a Plains (Island or Mountain only from Scalding Tarn - so no Plains available). Actually Scalding Tarn fetches Island or Mountain only. They also have Marsh Flats in hand which fetches Plains or Swamp. So the correct sequence is: play Marsh Flats as land drop, crack Marsh Flats for a Plains, then cast Ragavan, then attack with Ragavan with Ephemerate backup. Instead they're casting Ragavan before playing their land for the turn (Marsh Flats), which means they might not have white mana for Ephemerate if Ragavan gets targeted by removal.

Ragavan is on the opponent's battlefield and will attack, generating Treasure tokens and card advantage. Fatal Push cleanly kills it at MV 1. Prioritizing Emperor of Bones activation (which likely can't adapt again since it already has +1/+1 counters) over removing the opponent's primary threat is suboptimal.

Ragavan, Nimble Pilferer is on the opponent's battlefield. Pithing Needle names Ragavan, which only shuts off activated abilities (Dash from hand). Ragavan's combat damage trigger is a triggered ability, not an activated ability, so Pithing Needle doesn't stop it. Ragavan is about to attack and generate value (Treasure + exile a card). Fatal Push costs B and can destroy Ragavan (mana value 1, well within the 2-or-less threshold). Gem25F Coach has Swamp and Ifnir Deadlands available to cast it. Killing Ragavan now before combat prevents the opponent from getting a Treasure token and card advantage from the combat damage trigger.

annotation_description: Fetched Meticulous Archive (enters tapped, surveil 1) instead of an untapped land. With Solitude and Ephemerate in hand, having untapped white mana available immediately could be relevant for casting Ephemerate or other instant-speed plays. The surveil 1 is marginal value compared to having mana available this turn.

Cast Ephemerate on Ragavan postcombat, which has no ETB trigger and provides essentially zero value. This wastes a key white card that could have been exiled to evoke Solitude, which would remove Emperor of Bones (a significant threat) and gain 3 life from lifelink. The opponent is at 6 life and Emperor of Bones is a dangerous recursive threat.

Cast Fatal Push (an instant) during precombat main phase targeting a tapped Ragavan, when there's no benefit to doing so before combat. Emperor of Bones wants to attack and use its beginning-of-combat exile trigger. Fatal Push could be held until after combat or even until the opponent's turn for maximum flexibility and information.

MiMo Villain declined to cast Ephemerate in response to Fatal Push targeting Ragavan. Ephemerate would save Ragavan by exiling and returning it (causing Fatal Push to fizzle), preserving a 2/1 attacker against an opponent at 6 life. Ephemerate also has Rebound, providing additional value next turn (potentially blinking an evoked Solitude). Letting Ragavan die wastes both a creature and the opportunity to use Ephemerate's rebound.

annotation_description: Exiling Ephemerate to pay for Solitude's evoke cost destroys the Solitude + Ephemerate combo, one of the most powerful interactions in Modern. The combo would allow flickering Solitude to dodge the evoke sacrifice, getting multiple ETB exile triggers and keeping a 3/2 lifelink body, plus rebound for another trigger next upkeep. Instead, both cards are lost for a single exile effect.

Declined to cast Kozilek's Command for X=1 during combat, missing an opportunity to scry 1 and draw a card (or create a chump blocker). With Eldrazi Temple (untapped, providing {C}{C} for Eldrazi spells) and Ifnir Deadlands (untapped, providing {C}), Coach had exactly 3 mana to cast Kozilek's Command at X=1. At 6 life in a precarious position, drawing an extra card is significant value.

Gem25F Coach passed their own main phase without casting their only card in hand, Kozilek's Command, which could have been cast for X=1 using Eldrazi Temple ({C}{C}) + Ifnir Deadlands ({C}). With no opposing creatures to worry about and being essentially hellbent, casting it for 'scry 1, draw a card' + 'create 1 Spawn token' would generate meaningful card advantage and board presence.

Gem25F Coach passed with Kozilek's Command as their only card in hand and 5 mana available (including Eldrazi Temple for the colorless costs). They could cast it for X=3, choosing 'Scry 3, draw a card' and 'Create 3 Eldrazi Spawn tokens' (or exile graveyard cards). With an empty hand after this and being at 10 life, drawing a card and creating tokens to equip Shadowspear for lifelink was critical. Instead they passed and skipped to no attacks with an empty board.

Gem25F Coach has Kozilek's Command in hand with 5 untapped lands (including Eldrazi Temple which produces CC for Eldrazi spells). With Eldrazi Temple providing {C}{C} plus Wastes providing {C}, they can cast Kozilek's Command for X=1 (costing {1}{C}{C}) or potentially X=2. The opponent has only a Treasure Token on board and the Coach has an empty hand after this. Kozilek's Command could be used to scry and draw a card (critical with an empty hand) plus exile creatures/cards from graveyards or create Spawn tokens. Passing the turn with the only card in hand uncast wastes mana and tempo, and leaves the Coach in topdeck mode with no board presence beyond equipment and lands.

Passed on casting Kozilek's Command at end of opponent's turn with all mana available and nothing else to spend it on. Could have cast it for X=4, creating 4 Eldrazi Spawn tokens and drawing a card (scry 4 + draw). This would develop a board presence, provide future mana from Spawn sacrifice abilities, and generate card advantage - all at instant speed with mana that would otherwise go completely unused.

Gem25F Coach passed without casting anything despite having Nethergoyf (a 5/6 for {B} given 5 card types in graveyard) and the opponent having zero creatures on board. This wastes a full turn of attacking with a massive threat while the opponent is at 11 life. They could also have cast Nethergoyf and still had mana available for Kozilek's Command.

Gem25F Coach passed priority with 5 mana available and two strong cards in hand. Nethergoyf would be a powerful threat here - with Thoughtseize (x3), Prismatic Vista, Mishra's Bauble, Fatal Push (x2), and Urza's Saga in the graveyard, that's at least 5 card types (sorcery, land, artifact, instant, enchantment), making Nethergoyf a 5/6. The opponent's board is empty of creatures, so deploying a 5/6 for just {B} is an incredible tempo play. Additionally, Kozilek's Command could also be cast with the remaining mana (X=3 with Eldrazi Temple contributing {C}{C}). Passing the turn with an empty board against an opponent at 11 life while holding these threats is throwing away a winning position.

Gem25F Coach declined to cast Kozilek's Command at the end of the opponent's turn (or during precombat main), despite having 5 lands available including Eldrazi Temple (which provides CC for colorless Eldrazi spells). With Eldrazi Temple + 4 other lands, they could cast Kozilek's Command for X=3 (costing 3+CC, paid by 3 lands + Eldrazi Temple for CC). This could have been used to create 3 Eldrazi Spawn tokens and draw a card (scry 3, draw 1), or exile a creature with MV 3 or less, providing significant value. The reasoning mentions following 'continuous instruction to pass_priority' which appears to be a systematic error - the AI is following meta-instructions rather than making optimal gameplay decisions. Kozilek's Command is an instant and this is a strong opportunity to use it, especially with the Eldrazi Temple discount.

Gem25F Coach has 5 untapped lands (Ifnir Deadlands, Swamp, Wastes, Eldrazi Temple, Ifnir Deadlands) and could cast Kozilek's Command during the opponent's combat phase. With Eldrazi Temple providing {C}{C} for colorless Eldrazi spells, they could cast Kozilek's Command for X=3 (paying 3+{C}{C}, using Eldrazi Temple for the {C}{C}). This could create 3 Eldrazi Spawn tokens for blocking, or exile a creature with mana value 3 or less, or scry 3 and draw a card — all highly valuable at 10 life against an opponent at 11. Playing this as a combat trick during the opponent's attack step is exactly when you want to use an instant like this. Instead, they passed priority and wasted a prime opportunity to use their mana.

Gem25F Coach passed priority in their own postcombat main phase without casting Nethergoyf (which would be a 5/6 given 5 card types in graveyard: sorcery, land, instant, artifact, enchantment) or Kozilek's Command. With the opponent at 11 life and no creatures on board, deploying a 5/6 threat is critical to applying pressure and closing the game.

Passed the entire precombat main phase without playing Prismatic Vista (free land drop) or casting Nethergoyf (a 5/6 for just {B}) when the opponent has zero creatures on board. Missing the land drop alone is a minor error, but declining to deploy a 5/6 threat for 1 mana against an empty board compounds the mistake significantly.

During combat, Gem25F Coach declined to use Kozilek's Command or Shadowspear. With 5 untapped lands (including Eldrazi Temple for {C}{C}), they could cast Kozilek's Command for X=1 or more to create Eldrazi Spawn tokens for blocking/mana, draw a card, or exile creatures. The opponent is at 11 life and Coach is at 10 life with an empty board of creatures, so generating value or blockers could be important. However, since this is during Coach's own combat with no attackers declared, the timing may not matter much - they could cast it on the opponent's end step instead for the same effect. The Shadowspear activation to remove hexproof/indestructible also seems irrelevant here. This is borderline - saving Kozilek's Command for the opponent's end step or a more reactive moment could be correct.

Gem25F Coach passed priority with 5 untapped lands, holding Nethergoyf (which would be a large creature given 6+ card types in graveyard: sorcery, land, instant, artifact, enchantment = at least 5/6), Kozilek's Command, and Prismatic Vista. The board is empty of creatures, opponent is at 11 life, and Coach is at 10 life needing to establish a clock. Passing here wastes an entire turn's worth of mana and development. At minimum, playing Prismatic Vista (free land drop) and casting Nethergoyf (a massive threat) would apply significant pressure. The reasoning even acknowledges these are the correct plays but then passes anyway.

Passed priority with an empty opponent board when holding Nethergoyf (a 4/5 for B given 4 card types in graveyard) and Kozilek's Command for card advantage/tokens, plus an unplayed Prismatic Vista land drop. This is the ideal window to deploy threats and generate value while the opponent has no board presence.

Prismatic Vista could be played as a land drop. Instead, the player passed priority doing nothing, wasting mana and missing an opportunity to develop their board when the opponent has no threats in play.

Gem25F Coach has Kozilek's Command in hand with access to at least 5 mana (including Eldrazi Temple for {C}{C}). During MiMo Villain's combat step, this could be cast as an instant to create Eldrazi Spawn tokens as blockers or to draw cards. MiMo Villain has no creatures on board currently, so the immediate combat threat may be nil, but the reasoning given ('following a consistent pattern of passing') suggests the AI is not actually evaluating the game state. If MiMo Villain has no attackers, passing is fine, but the reasoning is suspect and Kozilek's Command at end of opponent's turn for card draw would be valuable if not used now.

The reasoning given ('pass to ensure game progression per instructions') is not a valid strategic reason - it's following a flawed directive that causes them to waste mana and miss developing their board in a close game at 10-10 life.

Activating Prismatic Vista before casting Thought-Knot Seer when they already had enough mana to cast TKS. Paying 1 life unnecessarily before seeing the opponent's hand (via TKS's ETB) means they lose information that could inform whether the life point matters. The extra land isn't needed this turn since they already have sufficient mana for TKS.

Cast Thought-Knot Seer when the opponent appears to have an empty hand, wasting its powerful ETB hand disruption ability. The surveil is more impactful in this top-deck mode.

There's no reason to hold this spell with an empty hand and no better timing consideration.
